content: Toxic Oil Syndrome (TOS) was the name given to a peculiar disease outbreak that occurred in Spain in 1981. Initially, the disease presented as a lung condition with unusual characteristics. Although the symptoms resembled those of a lung infection, they did not respond to antibiotic treatment, which is typically effective for such infections. The disease appeared to be geographically localized, affecting specific areas, and it was observed that multiple members of the same family could fall ill while their neighbors remained unaffected. After the acute phase of the illness, patients exhibited a variety of chronic symptoms. Investigations eventually identified the cause of the syndrome as the consumption of rapeseed oil that was originally intended for industrial purposes rather than for human consumption. This oil had been imported as a low-cost industrial product by the company RAPSA in San Sebastián, processed by RAELCA, and refined by ITH in Seville. It was then fraudulently sold as olive oil by street vendors at local markets, where it was purchased for use in cooking and salads. The prevailing hypothesis is that toxic compounds were formed during the refining process, which was used to remove aniline—a chemical added to denature oils meant for industrial use. Once the source of the outbreak was identified, public health authorities implemented a program allowing individuals who had purchased the contaminated oil to exchange it for genuine olive oil. This intervention effectively brought the outbreak to an end. The conclusion that the contaminated oil was the cause of TOS is supported by robust epidemiological evidence. However, experimental studies conducted on various laboratory animals have not been able to replicate the symptoms observed in human cases of TOS. Neither in vivo nor in vitro studies using specific toxic components of the oil, such as fatty acid anilides and esters of PAP (phenylaminopropane), have demonstrated a causal link to the pathogenesis of the syndrome. The fact that the initial cases of TOS were reported in Madrid, near the U.S. military base in Torrejón de Ardoz, coupled with the secrecy surrounding the extensive investigations, fueled conspiracy theories about the origins of the syndrome.
